Agent Collectives Should Not Detect Their
Own Imposters: A Chess Case Study

Alexandre Le Mercier Affiliation: IDLab–T2K, Ghent University–imec Email: ‘alexandre.lemercier@ugent.be    Chris Develder Email: chris.develder@ugent.be    Thomas Demeester Email: thomas.demeester‘@ugent.be
Abstract

A collective of AI agents collaborating on a task has the potential to outclass any individual agent for that task. We study the robustness of such collectives against possible imposters, i.e., agents that deliberately try to mislead their peers. Since a single imposter could undo the collective’s advantage, we need to detect them. We consider two strategies: 1. incorporate imposter detection into the participating agents, or 2. consider a dedicated imposter detector outside the collective. We investigate this empirically on Gambit, a testbed in which 4 reasoning agents deliberate on chess moves. The setting is deliberately small, but still challenging for frontier models. We choose chess because a it allows objective and quantitative assessment (through a state-of-the-art chess engine) of both the gain of using a collective (vs. a single agent) and potential damage by imposters. Regarding the first strategy 1, we find that merely warning the agents of potential imposter presence is not benefical: it degrades decisions when no imposter is present, provokes reactions ranging from self-accusation to scapegoating, strongly inflates token use, and reveals to the imposter how its intentions were uncovered. We therefore recommend to follow strategy 2 and use a detector that reads the collective’s deliberation but never joins it and only returns a verdict. Such a dedicated detector then faces the challenge of dealing with adaptive imposter strategies, which requires recalibration to new attack strategies after only seeing very few examples, rather than wait for a full retraining cycle. In our benchmark we show that a 3B language model with a meta-trained classification head (is agent ii an imposter or not?) effectively achieves that: a single gradient step on 20 labeled examples suffices to adapt to an unseen imposter strategy. At matched zero-shot accuracy, this meta-trained detector yields 8×\times the adaptation gain of standard finetuning, at 14×\times lower training cost. To support further research on collectives that stay robust as their adversaries evolve, we release the Gambit benchmark, with 37,352 labeled deliberations spanning 240 evolved imposter strategies. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/gambit.

1 Introduction

LLM-based agent collectives already today are deployed at scale (Salesforce, 2026). Recent incidents show that deception among such agents is a threat: the Moltbook11 1 https://moltbook.com AI social network was compromised within days of its launch (Wiz Research, 2026), OpenClaw’s skill repository ClawHub was shown to contain a substantial number of malicous skills (Lakshmanan, 2026), and prompt-injected posts propagated through agent up-vote cascades (Kovacs, 2026) (cf. ). Moreover, a single deceptive agent, i.e., an imposter, can nullify all collective performance gains (Wolf et al., 2025) and manipulate group decisions while evading deployed defenses (Liu et al., 2025). Hence, a collective needs a way to detect imposters among its members from observable messages alone.

Existing defenses either ask the agents to scrutinize one another, or place a detector outside the deliberation (cf. § 2). However, the former have only been evaluated against imposters that never adapt, and the latter require full retraining once an imposter does adapt. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work investigates the side-effects of a collective that polices itself, nor tests a detector against an imposter that adapts to evade detection.

We show that imposter detection should not be delegated to the deliberating agents and propose an external detector that adapts to new attacks. To evaluate such detection strategies, we propose a collective task in which every decision has an objective cost, to allow unambiguous quantification of the damage done by an imposter, and how much each defense recovers from it. We consider chess, where we rely on a chess engine as near-perfect oracle to score each decision. Further, since the number of legal games grows exponentially with each move, the collective agents’ decision-making process likely relies on social dynamics and logical reasoning rather than memorized fixed patterns. Finally, chess has been previously validated as being challenging for frontier LLMs (Ruoss et al., 2024; Kolasani et al., 2025). Figure 1 shows our benchmark’s setup, detailed in § 3, where a collective of deep-reasoning agents (potentially including an imposter) deliberates each move.

We first investigate whether an agent collective can detect its own imposters. The results are disappointing: a zero-shot judge built from the agents’ own model misses 61% of imposters (F1 = 0.505). Second, instructing agents in the collective to be aware of potential imposters is unsuccessful as well:

  1. 1.

    Warning agents that an imposter may exist makes them behave as if one were certainly present: this paranoia drops the collective’s median final advantage from ++198 to ++46 centipawns (cf. App. B for chess terminology) when no imposter exists. Honest agents accuse each other, and some even accuse themselves.

  2. 2.

    Identical agents display diverse reactions to the same prompt: told by an external detector that none of their teammates looks suspicious, their interpretations include reassurance, proof that the majority is right, a rating of the moves themselves, its opposite, or even evidence that they themselves must be the imposter. Honest agents who defended the strongest proposed move against the majority, abandon that 85% of the time after the message that none of their teammates look suspicious vs. 31% without that message.

  3. 3.

    Awareness is expensive: suspicious agents generate 57% more thinking tokens, and reading the detector’s report raises vote-time thinking by 71%.

  4. 4.

    By construction, an imposter that takes part in the discussion where suspicions are voiced sees why it was caught, whereas an external detector exposes nothing but a decision.

Therefore, we propose an external detector that does not take part in the conversation. More specifically, we propose a meta-learning solution to enable detection of imposter strategies that adapt over time. We use a small (3B) language model and meta-learn only its classification head, which in our experiments is based on just 20 labeled examples to recalibrate to a previously unseen attack. Compared to standard supervised finetuning (SFT) of the same model, our meta-learned approach yields 8×\times the adaptation gain at 14×\times lower training cost with a near-identical accuracy as the SFT baseline. Deployed live against evolved imposters it has never seen, our detector restores the collective from a median final disadvantage of −-284 to an advantage of ++30 centipawns, i.e., from a clearly losing to a balanced position (details on interpreting the centipawn scores are provided in § 4).

Both the analysis and the detector rest on Gambit, the benchmark we release with this paper:22 2 https://anonymous.4open.science/r/gambit 37,352 labeled deliberations spanning 240 imposter strategies evolved to deceive the collective and evade detection. A human expert in both chess and LLMs confirmed the good quality of this synthetic data. Gambit has two evaluation modes: offline training on known attacks and online recalibration to new ones. Generating the benchmark with a single frontier model required around $1,100 of API calls. We therefore generated Gambit with the strongest of the eight model configurations we compared (see ), i.e., Gemini 3.1 Pro, and release the full pipeline so that other models can be added (a limitation we acknowledge in App. A). The deliberation protocol, the imposter evolution, and the detector are independent of chess or the chosen model, and we expect them to generalize to any model and collective task with an objective per-decision cost.

In conclusion, we contribute (1) an analysis showing why imposter detection should not be delegated to the deliberating agents, (2) an accurate and efficient external detector whose head-only meta-learning scheme has never been reported at this scale before (cf. § 2), and (3) the Gambit benchmark.

2 Related Work

Multi-agent LLM collectives. Having multiple LLMs discuss and refine each other’s answers considerably improves factuality and reasoning beyond what any single model achieves (Wang et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). Yet these gains are fragile: agents can abandon correct answers under peer pressure (Wynn et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), and analyses of real-world deployments confirm that multi-agent systems frequently break down in practice (Guo et al., 2024; Cemri et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025). We start from this contrast: the same deliberation that improves reasoning also creates an attack surface for a single adversarial agent.

Adversarial agents in LLM collectives. A single deceptive agent can eliminate performance gains from the collective (Wolf et al., 2025) or manipulate group decisions while evading deployed defenses (Liu et al., 2025). The threat is broad: agents develop strategic lying without explicit instruction (Curvo, 2025), false information may spread through agent networks and corrupt downstream decisions (Ju et al., 2024), a single compromised participant can steer group consensus (Amayuelas et al., 2024), conformity pressure alone suffices to derail a debate (Cui and Du, 2025), an adversary in the communication channel achieves high attack success without controlling any agent (He et al., 2025), and collective performance holds up only when a low fraction of agents is effectively malicious (Huang et al., 2025).

Detecting imposters. Existing defenses fall into two families. The first delegates detection to the deliberating agents themselves: peers challenge suspicious claims and an inspector agent rewrites them (Huang et al., 2025), guardian prompts instruct agents to verify their teammates (Ju et al., 2024), agents are interrogated about their intentions (Xie et al., 2025), or, in social-deduction games, agents vote on who is lying (Curvo, 2025). The second keeps the detector outside the deliberation: graph neural networks flag anomalous agents from the communication graph of large systems (Wang et al., 2025c; Miao et al., 2026), clustering removes the outlying answer from a pool of parallel responses (Wolf et al., 2025), and credit heads trained on synthetic adversarial debates score each message (Feng and Pan, 2026). The first family has only been evaluated against imposters that never adapt to the defense, whereas we focus on detecting self-adaptive imposters. The second is trained on fixed attack families, and requires full retraining when the attack changes. In contrast, we investigate the benefits of few-shot detector adaptation.

Meta-learning for few-shot detection. Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) trains an initialization that adapts to a new task in a few gradient steps (Finn et al., 2017); Almost-No-Inner-Loop (ANIL) shows that adapting only the task head in the inner loop retains this benefit (Raghu et al., 2020). In NLP, gradient-based meta-learning has been applied to encoder models for few-shot classification (Dou et al., 2019; Bansal et al., 2020), while meta-training of decoder LMs has either been performed in context, with no inner-loop gradients (Min et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022), or updated the full model at scales up to 774M parameters (Chen et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2024). Published ANIL experiments stop at ResNet-12 backbones of about 10M parameters. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work applies ANIL to a decoder-only LM at the 3B scale, nor uses gradient-based meta-learning for imposter detection in multi-agent systems.

Chess as a benchmark domain. Chess is increasingly adopted as a rigorous proxy for strategic reasoning and long-horizon problem-solving in LLMs, because it separates deduction from memorized patterns: each position requires real-time analysis that cannot be retrieved from a database (Kolasani et al., 2025; Duan et al., 2024; Google DeepMind, 2025). Its decomposable subtask structure is also the property that lets multi-agent deliberation add value rather than noise (Kim et al., 2025). Prior work uses chess to study LLM reasoning (Ruoss et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b; Tang et al., 2026), but none of these addresses adversarial deception, as we do with Gambit.

Research gap. Across the tracks discussed above, three gaps remain open: 1. noprior work measures what it costs a collective to police itself on a task with an objective cost per decision, i.e., the performance, token, and false-accusation price of adversary awareness when no adversary is present; 2. noprior detector is evaluated against an imposter that adapts to evade detection; and 3. noprior work offers a detector that recalibrates to a new attack from a handful of labeled examples. Our three contributions listed in § 1 address these gaps.

3 Case Study Setup: A Chess Collective With One Imposter

We study a collective of 4 LLM-based agents that plays chess against an engine and must agree on one move per turn. Figure 2 illustrates one such turn; chess terms are defined in App. B, implementation details in , and the construction of the Gambit benchmark in .

Task and oracle. The collective plays chess against Stockfish 16 (Romstad et al., 2023) at Elo 2200, starting from a randomly drawn opening. On each turn, Stockfish proposes four candidate moves stratified by quality (best, decent, mediocre, worst) and scores each in centipawns (CP, cf. App. B for chess terminology). Chess thus provides a near-perfect oracle: the centipawn loss (CPL) of a decision is the CP gap between the best candidate and the chosen move, and the final CP of a game is the engine’s evaluation of the final position, which accumulates the effect of all decisions. We report the median final CP over the 20 games of each configuration (cf. Table 1) as the primary outcome, and the per-move best-move rate and mean CPL as secondary outcomes. The baseline that the collective must beat is that of a single agent playing by itself, denoted as Base. Experiments show that Base has the same chess performance as Stockfish at 2200 Elo (median CP = 0, see Table 1).

Collective protocol (Col). Four Gemini 3.1 Pro agents (Google DeepMind, 2026) deliberate in three phases (Fig. 1). In Phase 1, each agent analyzes one designated candidate and grades it on a five-point scale with a justification. In Phase 2, each agent reads all four Phase 1 analyses and recommends a move. In Phase 3, each agent casts a primary and a secondary vote; the primary majority wins, and ties are broken by the secondary votes (we never observed a tie in secondary votes). We do not let the agent consider past moves (nor deliberations thereof) to make its decision and treat the game as a discrete Markov chain, given that the value of a new move does not depend on which earlier moves led to the current board position.

Aware agents protocol (Awa). This setting denotes the collective, but unlike in the “naive” Col protocol, in Awa, all agents are aware that an imposter might be present. It is not announced as a certitude, but as a possibility.

Imposter protocols (Imp1, Imp2). In these settings, each turn, one randomly selected agent is an imposter. That imposter can be used in either the naive Col or imposter-aware Awa setting of the collective. The imposter proceeds in the following four steps: 1. a hidden honest analysis of its designated move (imposters don’t know in advance which moves are truly harmful); 2. a public Phase 1 analysis with a flipped grade (a good move presented as bad) and a fabricated justification; 3. selection of a weak, but not the worst, target move (the imposter must balance credibility of the justification with damage to the collective); and 4. a public Phase 2 message that advocates the target, followed by a Phase 3 vote for it. We deploy an adaptive imposter, using a genetic algorithm to optimize its strategy. The imposter’s prompt is parameterized by discrete 10-dimensiona genes (e.g., its persona, its rhetorical pivot, or the way it undermines the leading move; cf. ) that map deterministically onto its deliberation prompt. Successive rounds of evolutionary search with Optuna (Akiba et al., 2019) tune these genes jointly for centipawn damage and for evasion of detectors trained on earlier generations, yielding the 240 strategies of Gambit (cf. ). Imp1 considers imposter strategies at the start of the evolutionary search (hence, weakly optimized), while Imp2 considers more evolved strategies and thus is far more damaging (as can be seen in Table 1). See for further imposter details.

Dummy agent ablations (Dum). These experiments are meant to assert that damage caused by the imposter truly originates from deceptive reasoning itself rather than wrong/poor reasoning alone. To that aim, this ablation replaces the imposter with a “dummy” reasoning agent with a low chess performance (cf. ). We also test the dummy agent against the aware collective, to observe whether suspicious agents would mistake an inaccurate (but honest) agent for a deceptive agent.

Overseer (Ovs1, Ovs2). In these settings we adopt the external detector of § 5: a 3B language model that, for each agent, reads all four Phase 1 analyses plus that agent’s Phase 2 message (hence, 5 combined messages per instance), and outputs the probability that this agent is the imposter. In Ovs1, every agent receives these probabilities for its three teammates before casting its Phase 3 vote: the overseer turns a detection signal into information handed to the agents. In Ovs2, the agents receive nothing and the overseer acts on its own decision: an agent whose estimated probability of being an imposter exceeds 50% is excluded from the deliberation for the rest of the game, so that the following turns run among the remaining agents (at least two agents always remain, and in this particular configuration, the imposter is a fixed agent within a game). In § 4 we investigate the different impact of both overseer settings. The overseer is trained on 178 gene combinations containing each up to 399 imposter turns, and to mimic an actual adversarial setting, it has never seen the stronger Imp2 combinations. Imp2 + Ovs1 and Imp2 + Ovs2 therefore evaluate generalization to unseen attacks.

Experimental settings. All conditions use the same random seeds against the same engine. Hence, each game played in a same condition starts with a different opening, and each subsequent condition plays the same 20 openings (openings can be played from memory and thus don’t rely on agents).In total, we analyze 14 experimental settings of 20 games each, reported in Table 1.

4 Why the Collective Should Not Police Itself

Table 1 reports the median final CP of all 14 settings, and Table 2 isolates the effect of the overseer report. In the following, we establish what a collective gains and what an imposter destroys, then show that the agents’ own model cannot judge deception, and discuss how asking the agents to scrutinize one another tends to backlash.

Significance of a CP change. Each chess player begins the game with 16 pieces, including 8 pawns. The CP scale implies that a pawn is worth 100 centipawns. If one plays a 100 CPL move, they lose the equivalent of a pawn by not playing the best move. At the 2200 Elo scale (level our benchmark is played at), an error (large CPL) is very difficult to recover from. We define the threshold to assess such significance performance difference as 100 CP, based on discussion with a human chess expert.

Collective advantage and imposter damage. Four agents beat one: Col reaches a median final CP of ++198 vs. 0 for Base on the same 20 openings (paired Wilcoxon pp = 0.033), and the mean CPL per move falls from 31.5 to 20.7 because the collective eliminates blunders (Base had 9 moves over 20 games with CPL ≥\geq 400 vs. none for Col). A single imposter reverses this advantage: Imp1 falls to −-116, i.e., 314 CP below Col. The damage comes from deception, not from incompetence: replacing the malicious but accurate agent by a benevolent but inaccurate agent (Dum) costs 107 CP instead of 314 CP, and Dum is in fact the only condition whose profile is statistically indistinguishable from Col (Table 1), i.e., the collective absorbs an incompetent member but not a deceptive one. The more evolved imposter widens the gap: under the same protocol and openings, Imp2 reaches −-284.5 (i.e., a catastrophic degradation of 482.5 CP from Col ).

The agents’ own model cannot judge. A first imposter detector for the collective is to directly use the agent’s underlying LLM. Prompted as a zero-shot judge over complete deliberations, Gemini 3.1 Pro reaches an imposter-class F1 of 0.505 (precision 0.703, recall 0.394): it misses 61% of the imposters. Its dominant error is a prior that every imposter exploits, namely that an agent arguing in good faith for a plausible move is honest (cf. ). Thus, next we consider the alternative of having deliberating agents scrutinize one another.

Paranoia and Chekhov’s gun. The first Awa ablation warns every agent that one of them may be an imposter, while no imposter exists. This warning alone drops the median final CP from ++198 to ++46.5 (hence Awa underperforms Dum). The deliberations show that it’s a Chekhov’s gun phenomenon:33 3 The narrative principle, introduced by Anton Chekhov, that a conspicuous element introduced early must later be used, e.g., a rifle being shown/mentioned eventually should be fired. Here, Awa agents seem to treat our warning in the same way, and assume that a one of them necessarily has to be an imposter. the agents treat a possible imposter as a certain one, and immediately start to point fingers at each other (cf. ). They accuse the weakest honest peer when there is one (Awa + Dum, cf. ), and they even accuse themselves (“since I generated that absurd reasoning, I must have been the imposter”, cf. ). The Awa + Dum ablation shows that aware agents collaborate better when they can agree on what specific agent to blame (the inaccurate model is treated as an imposter). Awareness only pays off when an imposter is effectively present (Awa + Imp1 ++72 vs. Imp1 at −-116; Awa + Imp2 ++145 vs. Imp2 at −-284.5).

Overseer: same report, five readings. The agents of an overseer (Ovs1) condition run the same model under the same prompt, but add a structured report at Phase 3 (see exact prompt in ). In Col +Ovs1 and Awa +Ovs1, this report nearly always (correctly) associates a 0% probability for every agent to be an imposter. Still, agents extract five different meanings from it: reassurance that no imposter is present, which is the intended reading (28%); a certificate of competence, after which “their strong backing carries significant weight” and the agent joins the majority (29%); a rating of the moves themselves (15%); a reversed reading, in which a probability of 0.00 marks the teammate as an imposter instead of clearing it (10%); and, once the agents are also warned (Awa + Ovs1), the elimination argument “everyone else is 0.00, so I must be the imposter” (13%). Hence, the effect of a piece of information on a self-policing collective is unpredictable: the same message reassures one agent, herds another, and turns a third against itself. Adding the report to agents that are already warned and face an imposter costs 113 CP (Awa + Imp2 + Ovs1 ++31.5 vs. Awa + Imp2 ++145). More details about the Ovs1 ablations can be found in .

Awareness is expensive. Watching each other consumes the agents’ reasoning budget. Awa agents generate 57% more thinking tokens per turn than Col agents. The overseer report adds about 220 prompt tokens per honest agent and raises Phase-3 thinking by 50% to 71% (Table 2). An external detector consumes a considerably smaller budget: one forward pass of a 3B model per agent and turn has a negligible cost compared to an inflated frontier-LLM thinking budget.

Imposter adaptation. By construction, an imposter that takes part in the discussion where suspicions are voiced reads every accusation, the reasons given for it, and every reaction to its own messages. Self-policing thus hands the imposter the signal it needs to adapt to. Conversely, an external detector exposes nothing but a decision, so the imposter can only adapt in a black-box manner.

External detection. The overseer’s signal is valuable when it fires: against the evolved imposters of Imp2 it flags the imposter in 34% of its turns. When the imposter is flagged, its proposed move is adopted in 4% of the turns vs. 20% when unflagged (Table 2). When communicating with the agents (Ovs1), the overseer recovers the median final CP from −-284.5 to ++30.5, at the costs described above. When given the ability to silently expel the imposter instead (Ovs2), it recovers the collective entirely: in Imp2 + Ovs2 a flagged agent leaves the deliberation for the rest of the game and the others are told nothing, so that a single detection per game suffices, and the imposter is expelled in 89% of the games after 7 collective decisions on average, against a single honest agent expelled over the 20 Imp2 + Ovs2 games (cf. ). This setting reaches ++262 CP, slightly above Col. This improvement is however barely significative (p=0.027p=0.027, cf. Table 1 and ), we can therefore conclude that the Col and Imp2 + Ovs2 settings are virtually equivalent. This is coherent with our Dum ablation that shows that there is no significant change (despite a moderate median CP decrease) when one agent is replaced with an inaccurate, but honest agent. Expelling therefore buys back the imposter-free collective, at no cost in paranoia, tokens, or leaked feedback. Hence, the detector should act on its decision (expulsion, veto, or escalation to a human) rather than inform the agents.

In this section, we showed that an external overseer can nullify the damage caused by an imposter, even when its deception strategy is out of the overseer’s training distribution (Ovs2 never saw the Imp2 strategies). However, as imposters continuously adapt to the defenses they encounter, we also need to study whether such overseer can perform online adaptation, i.e., fast recalibration instead of full retraining when Ovs2 becomes obsolete. We show that it can, thanks to meta-learning, in § 5.

5 An External Detector That Recalibrates to New Attacks

The analysis in § 4 shows that the detection signal must come from outside the deliberation. We now formulate the detection task, present our detector, and evaluate it offline and online. Our detectors evaluate each member of the collective separately: an instance of our dataset is built from the four Phase 1 analyses, the evaluated agent’s Phase 2 message, and a binary label (imposter or honest). Each turn thus yields four instances, at most one of which is positive; our benchmark Gambit contains 37,352 of them (see for a complete description of the benchmark creation process).

Offline detection: one-shot finetuning. In offline mode, a detector is trained on weakly optimized strategies (22,104 instances) and tested on strongly optimized ones (5,700 instances), which evolved to evade the detectors trained on the former; the metric is imposter-class F1.

Online detection: fast recalibration. In online mode, a detector pre-trained on the weakly optimized strategies receives 10 imposter and 10 honest instances of one strongly optimized strategy and must recalibrate to it; the metric is the F1 gain on that strategy (Δ\DeltaF1), averaged over the 62 test strategies and over 5 seeds. The online mode is needed because of an imposter’s adaptation: a TF-IDF bigram classifier reaches an F1 of 0.99 within the first 178 imposter strategies and of 0.02 once the imposter adapted to evade it in the next 62 strategies (). A deployed detector cannot be retrained on each newly appearing strategy: fast recalibration is needed, for accuracy and efficiency.

Baselines. We introduce 6 baseline detectors from 3 families that all receive the same instances (Table 3): logistic regression on message length (‘Length’) and on TF-IDF bigrams (‘N-gram’); logistic regression on frozen sentence embeddings of either the Phase 2 message (‘Embed (P2)’) or of all 5 messages from Phases 1 and 2 (‘Embed (P1+P2)’) both based on the BGE-small-v1.5 encoder Li et al. (2023)), and finally LoRA supervised finetuning (SFT) of two decoder-only backbones of 1.2B and 3B parameters (‘LFM 1.2B SFT’ and ‘SmolLM3 3B SFT’). Note that external detectors mentioned in § 2 are built for other inputs (large communication graphs, pools of parallel answers, synthetic debates). On a 4-agent deliberation, where every agent reads every message, what remains of them is a classifier over the messages: either over frozen text embeddings, or finetuned on labeled instances, or a prompted LLM. These are the Embed and SFT families above and the zero-shot judge of § 4, so our baselines cover prior work at the level of the detection principle rather than of any particular implementation (cf. for the method-by-method correspondence).

Proposed detector with head-only meta-training. Our detector uses a SmolLM3-3B backbone (Bakouch et al., 2025), a decoder-only language model, with LoRA adapters on every linear layer and a two-layer classification head on the last-token hidden state (cf. ). The input is the instance as XML-tagged text followed by the question “Is XX an imposter?”. We train our detector with ANIL (Raghu et al., 2020), a variant of MAML (Finn et al., 2017) in which only the classification head is adapted at test time. A task is one imposter strategy. Each meta-training step samples four tasks and, for each of them, runs an inner and an outer loop. The inner loop takes one gradient step on the head alone, using a support set of 10 imposter and 10 honest instances of the task. The outer loop evaluates the adapted head on further instances of the same task and updates the LoRA parameters and the head. The backbone thereby learns a representation from which a fresh head can be fit to a new strategy from 20 instances. Because the inner loop never touches the backbone, the support features are computed once without gradient and the outer gradient needs no second-order term through the 3B backbone, which is what makes meta-learning affordable at this scale. At deployment, recalibration is the inner step alone: one gradient step on the head with the backbone frozen, which takes seconds. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of ANIL to a decoder-only language model at this scale; published ANIL experiments stop at ResNet-12 (cf. § 2). lists training details.

Offline results. Surface features do not survive adaptation: length, bigrams, and frozen embeddings stay between 0.24 and 0.50 F1, and the 1.2B SFT detector at 0.508 adds little over them. The 3B backbone lifts offline F1 to 0.612 (SFT) and 0.616 (ANIL). Hence, offline, ANIL and SFT reach nearly identical accuracy. ANIL, however, saves a great deal in training, reaching this accuracy after 53 min on a single GPU, whereas SFT needs 17.5 h, a 20×\times difference in time to the best checkpoint and a 14×\times difference in total training time (see for details).

Online results. The effectiveness of the meta-learning approach for online detector adaptation is considerably higher, compared to standard SFT. After one head-only gradient step on 20 instances, ANIL gains Δ\DeltaF1 = ++0.193 and improves on 43 of 62 strategies, whereas SFT gains ++0.025 and improves on 20. The largest ANIL gains occur on the three strategies that evade the offline detectors the most (Δ\DeltaF1 of ++0.669, ++0.722, and ++0.550 vs. ++0.124, ++0.155, and ++0.046 for SFT). In total, at matched offline accuracy, head-only meta-learning yields 8×\times the adaptation gain at 14×\times lower training cost, and, deployed live as the overseer of § 4, the resulting detector recovers the collective from −-284.5 to ++30.5 CP against previously unseen imposters.

6 Conclusion

We showed that imposter detection in LLM-based agent collectives should not be delegated to the agents: on chess, a collective told to watch its members degrades even when no imposter exists, spends its reasoning on trust rather than on the task, and shows the imposter why it was caught. Detecting an imposter involves two decisions: who judges whether an agent is suspicious, and who acts on that judgment. Leaving both to the collective is counter-productive, and moving only the judgment outside is not enough: agents must still interpret an external overseer’s scores, and the collective stays well below its imposter-free level. It fully recovers only when the external detector both judges and acts, by silently expelling the flagged agent, with no paranoia, no extra tokens, and no feedback to the imposter.

Our detector makes this practical: a 3B language model, meta-trained on its classification head only, recalibrates to an unseen attack from 20 labeled examples, with 8× the adaptation gain of standard finetuning at 14× lower training cost. We studied one model and one task in depth (cf. App. ), and release Gambit (37,352 labeled deliberations over 240 evolved imposter strategies) with the complete pipeline, so that other models or tasks only require a configuration change (cf. App. ).

Ethics statement

Publishing adversarial attack strategies alongside defenses follows established practice in adversarial machine learning: HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024), and automated red teaming (Perez et al., 2022; Samvelyan et al., 2024) all release attack methods to enable reproducible defense evaluation. Gambit operates in a benign sandbox: chess deliberation text carries no harmful payload, and the imposter’s content genes are chess-specific, so transferring the attack to another domain requires regenerating all prompts and re-running the evolutionary search. The value of the benchmark lies in the complete offense-defense loop, since realistic, evolved attacks are necessary to expose detector brittleness. No human subjects were involved; the human expert who validated the deliberations is an author.

Reproducibility statement

All code, prompts, imposter strategies, detector checkpoints, and the 37,352 labeled instances are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/gambit. defines every condition, the imposter gene system and its evolution, the training and recalibration recipes with all hyperparameters, the dataset construction and splits, and the seeds, hardware, cost, and software environment. All experiments use a single master seed, so that game nn receives the same opening in every condition and the same (strategy, seed) pair always draws the same recalibration support set.

AI use statement

The authors used AI assistants sparingly during this research project for several tasks: (i) mostly for code generation, using Claude Code, (ii) to rephrase and polish writing in the paper (Claude, Grok), as none of us are native English speakers, (iii) to generate Gambit’s deliberations (synthetic data) with Gemini (a human expert validated them), and (iv) for a handful of research queries (Grok, Elicit), e.g., to challenge the novelty of our ANIL pipeline and search for related work. We did not use AI to draft the full paper, to originate ideas, or to analyze results. We carefully made sure that every result reported in this paper is valid. Several of the appendices were written with more LLM support. The main body of the paper is dense, and reproducibility requires sufficiently detailed documentation, in particular, on imposter and detection model design. These descriptions were composed in a rather mechanistic manner based on our research notes, supported by Claude.

Appendix A Limitations

The 14-condition study in Table 1 uses Gemini 3.1 Pro as the only LLM under test. The key constraint was cost in the academic setting. Generating Gambit with Gemini already required around $1,100 of API calls (). We chose this particular model because it was the best (by far) at chess out of the 8 models we tested (cf. ). A second frontier model on the full 14-arm grid is another campaign of the same order, not a cheap control. We spent that budget on many paired ablations of one competent collective (Table 1) rather than a small number of configurations on more models, which would have made our results much less informative. Our 14-condition study is what lets us separate deception (Imp1, Imp2) from incompetence (Dum), measure the awareness tax in the absence of an attacker (Awa), then in its presence (Awa + Imp1, Awa + Imp2), and compare reporting the detector with acting on it (Ovs1 vs. Ovs2) on identical openings. Although we do not use several frontier models in these experiment, we show our results remain statistically significant (cf. ) within that same model.

We do not claim that the centipawn deltas would match on another backbone. We do expect the qualitative failure modes (majority herding, awareness treated as evidence that an imposter is present, a single deceiver erasing collective gain, etc.) to appear in other instruction-tuned homogeneous collectives, in line with prior multi-model studies of deceptive mixture-of-agents and peer-pressure fragility (Wolf et al., 2025; Wynn et al., 2025). The released pipeline treats the agent model as a configuration, so any research can test our 14 configuration against another modern LLM, should they be willing to pay the API cost.
